title: The Thiele Machine: A Computational Model with Explicit Structural Cost
description:
I didn't invent a machine. I found one. That is my conviction. The Thiele Machine is how I put it on the table: an executable argument about which distinctions an account of computation should preserve.

A computation gives you an answer. What did it establish on the way there? Which distinctions did it keep? What did it cost to establish them? Certification is one point I could pin down. The machine carries structural state, a cost ledger, and rules for particular events. Its proofs show exactly what specified observations lose. A full encoding can preserve those distinctions; the question is which ones our models should keep.

The formal development includes accounting laws for systems satisfying A2, pricing adequacy for designated events, ledger uniqueness for a fixed schedule, observation adequacy, and exact conditions for descent from instruction traces to reachable-state simulations. A finite family of unit event floors can share one charge. Retaining history makes a deterministic step injective without changing its observed transition. Those are mathematical answers with explicit premises.

The repository contains the Coq kernel, an extracted OCaml runner, a Kami/Bluespec/Verilog hardware development, the monograph, and the mathematical specification. The assumption receipt covers 12,336 statements: 5,520 are closed under the global context, 6,816 depend on standard-library axioms, and none depend on project-local or third-party axioms. The standard-library dependencies use five named constants. Generic paid certification establishes accounting; semantic truth requires a sound checker. Hardware bridges retain their stated representation and compiler boundaries. The physical and foundational interpretations remain research questions.
